examples.2.1 Core loop: B.E.E.P. scans a room, spends one battery, places a pipe, and watches the air gauge climb within eight seconds. A session strings three eight-minute shifts into a 24-minute stop, ending with a crew radio line and a checkpoint; the long-term loop turns six repaired rooms into a self-sufficient outpost by shift 12. A missed shift rewinds to the last checkpoint, never the save.
examples.2.2 Player verbs and mechanics: Place is the primary verb: the player drags a pipe onto the 3×3 board, sees a ghost preview tint green or red, and confirms; it unlocks at shift 1 and feeds the air system. Reroute is secondary, arriving at shift 3 with branching paths, and it turns a straight-line fix into a network decision. Scan and choose cargo feed both verbs, while dismantle and overclock stay situational.
examples.2.3 Controls and camera: On iPad, the player taps a part, drags it to a tile, and twists two fingers to rotate; on PC, the same actions are left click, drag, and R. The camera stays fixed isometric with four snap angles and three zoom steps, and tap-to-feedback lands under 100 ms on the target tablet. Every action has a tap-only alternative and full remapping on keyboard and gamepad.
examples.2.4 Game modes and session structure: Campaign shift is the launch mode: one room, eight minutes, restore the air supply before the crew checks in. A session runs one to three shifts and ends at a summary screen; the game autosaves at every shift start and after each placement, so quitting mid-shift returns to the same camera and timer. There is no multiplayer at launch.
examples.2.5 Progression and unlocks: At 25 minutes, the player unlocks reroute and meets the first branching air path; the room is winnable with straight pipes, but the optional vent rewards a two-branch layout. By 70 minutes, overclock arrives with a power spike, and the final room at 110 minutes combines both without adding a new verb. The unlock graph gives every node one parent, except reroute, which needs both place and dismantle.
examples.2.6 Economy and resources: Air is the main resource: processing and tanks add 60 units per shift, three crew drain 24, and the cap is 100, so the player ends with 36 units and room for one optional repair. Power is tighter at 12 units per shift, with each fan costing 1; the player must choose between the grow lamp and the workshop. No resource can be bought with real money.
examples.2.7 Challenge, combat, and difficulty: The first real challenge is a leak in room 4: air drops 2 units per second, and the player must patch before rerouting, or the detour drains the tank. The room teaches order of operations, offers a hint after three fails, and rewinds to the shift start without deleting the discovered shortcut. No combat is in scope.
examples.2.8 Systems interaction matrix: Air owns pressure and leaks and reads filter parts from Cargo; Power owns charge and load, draws one unit per fan per shift, and reports brownouts to Crew. When a brownout hits, Air keeps its pressure value but stops production, so the two systems never write the same field. Systems owns Air and Power, Design owns Cargo, and Narrative owns Crew.
examples.2.9 Content and level design: The launch budget is six campaign rooms, twelve shift variants, ten radio beats, and three cosmetic sets, built by a four-person team in twelve weeks. Room 4, the leak, takes three days and teaches order of operations; its optional vent branch adds a route without a new asset. Critical path is six rooms and 96 minutes, or 3–4 hours with retries; three challenge variants add replay.
examples.2.10 Balance and tuning: Shift length defaults to eight minutes and is tunable from 4 to 12, owned by Design; air drain per crew defaults to 1.0 per minute, with a tested range of 0.5 to 2.0, owned by Systems. Every room_end event logs result, attempts, time, and air left, and the team reviews the dashboard every Friday. A designer can change values in the data file and rerun room 4 within a minute.
examples.2.11 First-time user experience (FTUE): At 0:00 B.E.E.P. wakes in the cargo bay with no timer; by 0:30 the player places one pipe, and at 1:30 the air gauge visibly climbs. At 2:30 a shortage forces a choice between two crates, and at 4:00 the tutorial shift ends with a summary and no lost progress. The crew radio call at 5:00 is skippable and subtitled; all five testers reached the summary without a prompt.
